The parabolas are
$(x-4)^2+(y-3)^2=x^2$ ...(i)
and $(x-4)^2+(y-3)^2=y^2$...
If point of intersection are $A  \left(x_1, y_1\right)$ and $B  \left(x_2, y_2\right)$ By solving (i) and (ii), we get

& (A B)^2=2\left(\left(x_1+x_2\right)^2-4 x_1 x_2\right)=192
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: One of the points of intersection of the curves $y=1+3 x-2 x^2$ and $y=\frac{1}{x}$ is  \left(\frac{1}{2}, 2\right)$. Let the area of the region enclosed by these curves be $\frac{1}{24}(l \sqrt{5}+\mathrm{m})-\mathrm{n} \log _{\mathrm{e}}(1+\sqrt{5})$, where $l, \mathrm{~m}, \mathrm{n} \in \mathbf{N}$. Then $l+\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{n}$ is equal to$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & A=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}}\left(1+3 x-2 x^2-\frac{1}{x}\right) \mathrm{dx} \\ & A=\left[x+\frac{3 x^2}{2}-\frac{2 x^3}{3}-\ln x\right]_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1+\sqrt{5}} \\ & A=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^2-\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^3-\ln \left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right) \\ & -\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)+\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)+\ln \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \\ & A=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}+\frac{3}{8}+\frac{3}{4} \sqrt{5}+\frac{15}{8}-\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{5} \\ & -\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{12}-\ln (1+\sqrt{5}) \\ & =\sqrt{5}\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{4}-\frac{2}{3}\right)+\frac{15}{8}-\frac{4}{3}+\frac{1}{12}-\ln (1+\sqrt{5}) \\ & =\frac{14}{24} \sqrt{5}+\frac{15}{24}-\ln (1+\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let $P$ be a variable point on the parabola $y = 4x^{2} + 1 .$~Then, the locus of the mid-point of the point $P$ and the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $P$ to the line $y = x$ is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
We have,

$y = 4x^{2} + 1$

$L: y = x$

Let the foot of perpendicular from~$P$~to line~$y = x$~is~$Q$.

Let~$P ≡ \left(x, y\right)$,~$Q ≡ \left(c, c\right)$~and~$R ≡ \left(h, k\right)$~where,~$R$~is the mid-point of~$PQ$.~

Clearly,

$PQ ⊥ L$

$⇒ $\dfrac{k - c}{h - c} = -$1$

$⇒ c = \left(\dfrac{h + k}{2}\right)

And,~

$R ≡ \left(\dfrac{x + c}{2}, \dfrac{y + c}{2}\right)$

$⇒ R ≡ \left(\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{h}{4} + \dfrac{k}{4}, \dfrac{y}{2} + \dfrac{h}{4} + \dfrac{k}{4}\right)

Hence,

$h = $\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{h}{4} + \dfrac{k}{4}$⇒ x = $\dfrac{3h}{2} - \dfrac{k}{2}

$k = $\dfrac{y}{2} + \dfrac{h}{4} + \dfrac{k}{4}$⇒ y = $\dfrac{3k}{2} - \dfrac{h}{2}

Now,

$y = 4x^{2} + 1$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{3k - h}{2}\right) =4 \left(\dfrac{3h - k}{2}\right)$2 + 1$

$⇒ \left($3k - h\right) = $2\left($3h - k\right)2 + 2$

Required locus is

2\left($3x - y\right)2 + \left($x - 3y\right) + 2 = 0$

$

questions.q: Let $P  \left(4, - 4\right)$ and $Q  \left(9, 6\right)$ be two points on the parabola, $y^{2} = 4x$ and let $X$ be any point on the arc $POQ$ of this parabola, where $O$ is the vertex of this parabola, such that the area of $∆ PXQ$ is maximum. Then this maximum area (in sq. units) is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Two different approaches we can use here.

Approach 1:

Let& $X$~be \left(t^{2}, 2t\right)$, then

Area of $\Delta PXQ = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{cases}t^{2} & 2t & 1 \\ 9 & 6 & 1 \\ 4 & - 4 & 1\end{cases}\right|$

$\Delta = \dfrac{1}{2} . 10 \left|t^{2} - t - 6\right| . . . \left($i\right)$

For maxima, differentiating both the sides with respect to~$t$~and equating it to~ zero, we get

${Δ}^{′} = 0 ⇒ $5 \left(2t - 1\right) = 0 ⇒ t = $\dfrac{1}{2}

Hence, area of $\Delta PXQ = 5\left|\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)2 - \dfrac{1}{2} -6\right| = 5\left|\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2} -6\right| = 5 \left|$\dfrac{1 - 2 - 24}{4}\right| = \dfrac{125}{4}~sq.units~(using equation \left(i\right)$)

Approach 2:

For maximum area tangent to the parabola at $X$ must be parallel to $PQ$. Let $X \left($t^{2}, 2t\right)$, then

2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} =$4 ⇒ $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2}{y}$⇒ $\$left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)\left(t^{2}, 2t\right) = \dfrac{1}{t}$

Also, slope of line $PQ = \dfrac{6 + 4}{9 - 4} =2$

Since, both the slopes are equal.

Thus,~$t = \dfrac{1}{2}⇒ X \left(\dfrac{1}{4},$1\right)$

Therefore, area of \Delta$PXQ = $\dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{cases}$4 & - 4 & 1 \\ $\dfrac{1}{4}$& 1 & 1 \\ 9 & 6 & 1\end{cases}\right| = $\dfrac{1}{2} \left|4\left(1 - 6\right) - \left(-4\right)\$left(\dfrac{1}{4} -$9\right) + 1\left(\dfrac{3}{2} -9\right)\right| = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|-20 - 35 - \dfrac{15}{2}\right| = \dfrac{125}{4}$& sq.units.

$

questions.q: The maximum area of a triangle whose one vertex is at $( 0, 0 )$ and the other two vertices lie on the curve $y = - 2x^{2} + 54$ at points $( x, y )$ and $( - x, y )$ where $y > 0$ is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let, area of triangle $ABC$ be denoted by $P$.

$⇒ P = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{cases}0 & 0 & 1 \\ x & y & 1 \\ - x & y & 1\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ P = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|0 - 0 + 2xy\right|$

$⇒ P = \left|xy\right|$

$⇒ P = \left|x\left(- 2x^{2} + 54\right)\right|$

$⇒ P = \left|- 2x^{3} + 54x\right|$

$⇒ \dfrac{dP}{dx} = \left|- 6x^{2} + 54\right|$

For critical points, $\dfrac{dP}{dx} = 0$

$⇒ \left|- 6x^{2} + 54\right| = 0$

$⇒ x = \pm 3$

So, the maximum area will be,

$A = 3 ( - 2 \times 9 + 54 )$

$⇒ A = 108$

questions.q: Let the latus rectum of the parabola $y^{2} = 4x$ be the common chord to the circles ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ each of them having radius $2\sqrt{5}$. Then, the distance between the centres of the circles ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$

Co-ordinates of focus of parabola will be& $S = \left(a, 0\right) = \left($1, 0\right)$.

Now, length of latus-rectum~$= 4$.

So,~length of semi latus-rectum~$= 2$.

Also,~$∠ LS{C}_{1} = 90 °$

Now, radius of circle~$L{C}_{1} = $2\sqrt{5}

Now, applying pythagoras theorem in~$△ LS{C}_{1}$,

\left($L{C}_{1}\right)2 = \left({C}_{1}$S\right)2 + \left($LS\right)2$

$⇒ \left({C}_{1}$S\right)2 = \left(L{C}_{1}\right)2 - \left(LS\right)2 = $\$lleft(2\sqrt{5}\right)$2 - \left($2\right)2 = 16$

$⇒ {C}_{1}S = $\sqrt{16} =$4$

$∴ {C}_{1}{C}_{2} = 2{C}_{1}S = 2 $\times$4 = 8$.

$

questions.q: If the shortest distance of the parabola $y^{2} = 4x$ from the centre of the circle $x^{2} + y^{2} - 4x - 16y + 64 = 0$ is $d$, then $d^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given: Equation of parabola is $y^{2} = 4x$ and the equation of circle is $x^{2} + y^{2} - 4x - 16y + 64 = 0$.

We know that, equation of normal to parabola is given by, $y = mx - 2m - m^{3}$.

Also, the centre of given circle is \left(2, 8\right)$.

The normal of parabola is passing through center of circle.

$⇒ 8 = 2m - 2m - m^{3}$

$⇒ m = - 2$

So point $P$ on parabola is given by,

\left({am}^{2}, - 2am\right) = ( 4, 4 )$

And $C = ( 2, 8 )$

$⇒ PC = \sqrt{4 + 16} = \sqrt{20}$

$d^{2} = 20.

$

questions.q: If the $x$-intercept of a focal chord of the parabola $y^{2} = 8x + 4y + 4$~is $3$, then the length of this chord is equal to _____ .
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$Given,

The $x$-intercept of a focal chord of the parabola $y^{2} = 8x + 4y + 4$~is $3$,

Now simplifying equation of~the given parabola we get,

$y^{2} = 8x + 4y + 4$

$⇒ \left(y - 2\right)2 = 8 \left($x + 1\right)$

Now on comparing with standard parabola~$y^{2} = 4ax$~we get,

$a = 2, X = x + 1, Y = y - 2$

Hence, the vertex is~ \left(-1, 2\right)$~and~focus is~ \left(1, 2\right)$

So, equation of line passing through focus is~given by~$y - 2 = m \left($x - 1\right)$

Now, putting \left($3, 0\right)$~{as given $x -$intercept of focal chord is $3}~in the above line we get,~$m = - 1$~

So, equation of chord will be~$y = 3 - x$,

Now putting the value of~$y = 3 - x$~in parabola~ \left(y - 2\right)2 = 8 \left($x + 1\right)$~we get,

$⇒ \left($1 - x\right)2 = 8 \left(x + 1\right)$

$⇒ x^{2} - 10x - 7 = 0$

$⇒ \left|{x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right| = $\sqrt{{10}^{2} + 4 \times 7} = \sqrt{128}

$⇒ \left|{y}_{1} - {y}_{2}\right| = \left|3 - {x}_{1} - \left(3 - {x}_{2}\right)\right| = \left|{x}_{2} - {x}_{1}\right| = $\sqrt{128}

Length of focal chord \sqrt{\left|{x}_{2} - {x}_{1}\right|2 + \left|{y}_{2} - {y}_{1}\right|2} = \sqrt{256} =$16$.

$

questions.q: If the point on the curve $y^{2} = 6x,$~nearest to the point  \left(3, \dfrac{3}{2}\right)$ is $( \alpha, \beta ) ,$~then $2 ( \alpha + \beta )$ is equal to _________.$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
We have,

$y^{2} = 6x$

Comparing with~$y^{2} = 4ax$, we get~$a = \dfrac{3}{2}$

Let the point on parabola be~$P ≡ \left(at^{2}, 2at\right) ≡ $\$left(\dfrac{3}{2}t^{2}, 3t\right)$.

Normal at point $P$~is

$tx + y = 3t + \dfrac{3}{2}t^{3}$

It passes through \left($3, \dfrac{3}{2}\right),$hence

$⇒ 3t + \dfrac{3}{2} =3t + \dfrac{3}{2}t^{3}$

$⇒ t^{3} = 1 ⇒ t = 1$

Hence,

$P ≡ \left(\dfrac{3}{2},$3\right) = ( $\alpha, \beta )

Therefore,

$2 ( $\alpha + \beta ) ==2\$left(\dfrac{3}{2} +$3\right) = 9

$
